newsitem.title: USA: Author denies his novel inspired Oklahoma attack.
newsitem.headline: Author denies his novel inspired Oklahoma attack.

text.p: The author of a right-wing novel that prosecutors have alleged was a virtual blueprint for the Oklahoma City bombing said he did not believe his book had influenced accused bomber Timothy McVeigh.

In an interview to be aired on CNN's "IMPACT" newsmagazine on Sunday night, William Pierce was asked if his novel "The Turner Diaries" could have inspired the April 19, 1995 on the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, which killed 168 people.

"I don't believe so. I think it's a mistake to say that people hate the government or that people bomb government buildings because of a politically incorrect novel I wrote 22 years ago," Pierce said.

"The Turner Diaries" begins with a truck bomb attack on the FBI headquarters in Washington, D.C., at 9:15 a.m. The time of day, the type of bomb and the target were all similar to the Oklahoma City attack.

Asked about the similarities, Pierce said, "No ... The ingredients were quite different. The explosive material used in my fictional account was ammonium nitrate and fuel oil -- the principle explosive used in the Oklahoma City bombing was nitro methane."

The prosecution in McVeigh's trial has portrayed him as a fanatic whose hatred of the government was fuelled by the way federal agents handled a siege at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, in 1993. Some 80 people died in a raging fire.
"A lot of people feel that a government should not be allowed to get away with massacring its own citizens without good cause the way the government did in Waco," Pierce said.

Asked if the Oklahoma City bombing had filled him with the same kind of outrage as Waco, Pierce said, "I suppose I was more outraged and in general I guess I'm much more concerned about killings done by the government than I am about killings done by individuals."
"We Know how to deal with individual terrorists, but what do you do when you have a terrorist government?" he said.
Meanwhile, in Denver the jury deliberated for a second day on Saturday, trying to decide whether the Gulf War veteran is a cold-blooded killer or a man wrongly accused.
McVeigh, 29, has pleaded not guilty to charges of conspiracy, bombing and first-degree murder of the eight federal agents killed in the blast.
Asked if he would regret it if it turned out that McVeigh were guilty and were to say he was inspired by "The Turner Diaries," Pierce said, "Yes, I would."
